title: The Didache's prayer (Didache 9)
hookLine: as this bread was scattered on the hills and gathered into one
tomorrow: why would a man beg his friends not to rescue him?

cards: A potluck table: tamales from one kitchen, rice from another, somebody's grandmother's cake. An hour ago this meal was scattered across a whole town. Now it's one table.
An old Christian handbook called the Didache has a prayer built on that same picture, only smaller: one loaf, and the grain it came from.

teach.b: Didache is Greek for teaching, and chapter nine is a thanksgiving over a cup and over broken bread. It thanks the Father for the life and knowledge made known through Jesus, his servant. Then the picture.

teach.h: SCATTERED ON THE HILLS, MADE ONE.
teach.b: As this broken bread was scattered over the hills and, gathered together, became one, so may your Church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom.
Grain from many hillsides; one loaf; people from everywhere, one Church. And it's honest about limits: the same chapter says only the baptized should eat and drink of this Eucharist.
Giving thanks over bread is something a neighbor tradition knows in its own words.

teach.h: WHO BRINGS FORTH BREAD FROM THE EARTH.
teach.b: In the Mishnah, a foundational book of Jewish law, the blessing over bread praises God who brings forth bread from the earth. Jews call it the hamotzi, and families say it over challah on Shabbat.
Some scholars hear Jewish meal blessings in the Didache's thanksgivings. Here's what's shared: before eating, both name God as the giver of bread.
Here's the honest difference. The hamotzi is said over bread at any meal, thanking God for what the earth brings forth.
The Didache's prayer is said over the bread of the Eucharist, gives thanks through Jesus, and asks for one thing more: that the scattered be gathered.

how: Catholics pray for the unity of the Church at Mass, and some prayers in today's liturgy echo the Didache's picture of scattered grain gathered into one bread.

games.q: your parish and a nearby synagogue run a food drive together, and you're asked for one line for the poster. which fits honestly?
o: "come to Mass and receive the Eucharist with us."
"from many fields, one loaf: neighbors gathered at one table."
"every faith says exactly the same grace."
games.why: both traditions thank God over bread, and the scattered-grain picture welcomes everyone to the table without pretending the prayers are the same, or offering a sacrament meant for the baptized.

practice: If there's bread or a cracker nearby, hold a small piece before eating it, and think of how many fields and hands it came from, scattered, now one piece in your palm; then eat it slowly.
With nothing nearby, hold an open hand and think of one meal that gathered people from different places. Those who pray can ask, as the Didache does, that the Church be gathered into one.

wordCard.voice: The Didache's prayer. Thanks over broken bread, and a plea that the Church be gathered from the ends of the earth.

orig.note: Greek: a broken piece. the Didache's word for the bread it gives thanks over, scattered and gathered into one.

carryVoice: Carry this: gathered into one, the way grain from many hills becomes a loaf. Sleep well.
